title: The Hours Between Three and Four
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Nobody in my household knows that I wake most nights, somewhere between three and four, to pray while everyone else is still deeply asleep.
Narrator: It began almost by accident, during a stretch of insomnia two years ago, when I decided the sleepless hours might as well be spent on something worthwhile.
Narrator: [carefully] What surprised me was how quickly it stopped feeling like a coping strategy and started feeling like the part of my day I actually looked forward to.
Narrator: My sister, who shares a wall with my room, occasionally asks whether I've been sleeping poorly, having heard faint movement through the wall at strange hours.
Narrator: [reflective] I usually just say I got up for water, which isn't exactly a lie, since I do drink a glass afterward, but it isn't the whole truth either.
Narrator: A friend at the mosque once encouraged me to mention it in our small study group, arguing that hearing about it might motivate other women to try it themselves.
Narrator: [honestly] I turned the idea over for days, genuinely unsure whether sharing it would inspire anyone or simply hollow something out that currently feels entirely mine.
Narrator: There's a particular stillness to praying while the rest of the city sleeps, unwatched, unrecorded, with no possibility of anyone's approval reaching me afterward.
Narrator: [gently] If I described it out loud, I suspect some tiny, dishonest part of me would start waking up partly to have something to say about it later.
Narrator: That's not a risk I'm willing to take with the one habit in my life that still feels completely uncontaminated by anyone else's opinion of me.
Narrator: [calmly] So for now, it stays quiet, between the dark room, the sound of my own voice, and whoever it is I'm actually speaking to at that hour.
Narrator: Some mornings I'm exhausted by breakfast, and I've stopped minding, because whatever I lose in sleep, I seem to gain back in something steadier and harder to name.

quiz.question: What does the narrator do most nights between three and four?
options: She wakes to pray while the rest of the household sleeps
She reads a book
She goes for a walk
She checks her phone
quiz.explanation: She wakes most nights between three and four to pray while everyone else is still deeply asleep.

options: A doctor recommended it
Her mother taught her as a child

She read about it online

That she mention the habit in their study group to motivate other women

quiz.question: Why did she decide not to share it?
options: She was too tired to explain
Her sister forbade her

She worried sharing it would hollow out something that currently feels entirely hers
quiz.explanation: She feared that speaking about it might make a small, dishonest part of her start doing it partly to have something to say later.

They feared less personal information would weaken accountability.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: A period of insomnia gradually became a quiet worship routine.

options: If nobody corrects it, this becomes the version of events everyone quietly accepts
She fears other people's admiration could alter her intention.

quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: She fears other people's admiration could alter her intention.

You did plenty of work refining it
What unsettled me wasn't the questions themselves
More recipients collected support directly and volunteers heard fewer rumours.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: She feels tired after sacrificing sleep for the private prayer.

quiz.question: How does she evaluate that loss of sleep?
options: I'll just reply privately to the director, thank her
The prayer gives her an inner steadiness that outweighs the fatigue.
The fasting itself hasn't changed at all
It must not take their privacy, voice, or right to receive help quietly.
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: The prayer gives her an inner steadiness that outweighs the fatigue.
